title: Acute Otitis Media: Antibiotic Prescribing Criteria

evidenceAudit.scope: Child or adult with acute otitis media: deciding between no antibiotic, back-up prescription and immediate antibiotic, analgesia, antibiotic choice and dose, safety-net advice and referral for complications. findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 2026-10-18.

Medicine list restructured into a branched decision pathway on 2026-10-18. Doses, routes, adjustments, monitoring, contraindications and sources are unchanged from authoring-standard-2026-10-18-tier3b-v1-live.
unverifiedSections: NICE NG91 gives paediatric doses by age band but no adult doses; adult amoxicillin 500 mg and clarithromycin 500 mg are from NHS Grampian only and the page gives no erythromycin, co-amoxiclav, pregnancy or penicillin-allergy advice for adults.
NICE says to consult the local microbiologist for penicillin allergy where clarithromycin is unsuitable, and the MHRA assessment for macrolides in pregnancy; neither was opened.
Paracetamol and ibuprofen are dosed by age or weight in NICE with no numbers; adult doses come from the NHS website in this batch for the sprain topic and are not repeated here.
The NHS Grampian page does not separate adult from child doses; the 500 mg doses are read as adult doses and child doses link to the British National Formulary for Children.
Symptoms and signs are general clinical features and are not listed in the extracts opened.
Source pages were read through automated page extraction rather than page-by-page in the original documents, so each figure should be spot-checked against the source during clinical review.
The Saudi Food and Drug Authority (SFDA) drug registration site could not be opened from this environment, so registration of each medicine was not verified; check hospital formulary.

Medicine pathway: branch entry criteria, preferred options and “use when” conditions were assigned from this topic's own indications and management steps. Confirm each against the cited guideline before clinical use.

pathophysiology.summary: Acute otitis media is infection of the middle ear that often settles without antibiotics. NICE reports that antibiotics make little difference to symptoms and that acute complications such as mastoiditis are rare with or without them. Otorrhoea (discharge) through a perforated drum and bilateral infection under 2 years identify children more likely to benefit. Complications are mastoiditis, meningitis, intracranial abscess, sinus thrombosis and facial nerve paralysis.

clinicalManagement.title: Assess and decide
actions: Exclude sepsis and complications; refer if present.
Offer regular paracetamol or ibuprofen dosed by age or weight, with maximum doses for severe pain.

clinicalManagement.title: Choose antibiotic strategy
actions: Consider no antibiotic or back-up prescription when less likely to benefit.
Consider no antibiotic, back-up or immediate antibiotic with otorrhoea or under 2 years with both ears affected.
Immediate antibiotic if very unwell, signs of more serious illness or high risk of complications.

clinicalManagement.title: Choose antibiotic
actions: First choice amoxicillin 5 to 7 days three times a day; clarithromycin for penicillin allergy; erythromycin in pregnancy; second choice co-amoxiclav if worse after 2 to 3 days.

clinicalManagement.title: Safety-net
actions: Seek help if symptoms worsen rapidly, do not improve within 3 days or the child becomes very unwell.
Review if no improvement within 7 days.

regimens.indication: First-choice antibiotic for acute otitis media
regimens.dose: 1 to 11 months 125 mg; 1 to 4 years 250 mg; 5 to 17 years 500 mg
adjustments: Doses are for average-size children; check the British National Formulary for Children.
No renal or hepatic adjustment is given in the page opened.
monitoring: Review if symptoms do not improve within 7 days or worsen at any time.
contraindications: Penicillin allergy: use clarithromycin, or erythromycin in pregnancy.
Further contraindications are not listed in the extract opened.
